verdict: The candidate passes every numbered acceptance criterion under live execution, and its citations into index.html are real. All ten pinned exports are present with exact arities; the six rigs match the ratified table field-for-field; weights sum to 100 and a 60k-roll sample lands within noise of 40/26/18/10/5/1; effectiveRuns returns 2 / 1 / 3 for the three hand-checkable cases; rollRig() returns literal null when PP_RIGS is emptied (verified against a patched copy); the globals grep returns six hits, all on comment lines. I spot-checked eighteen of the file's index.html anchors and every identifier resolves — RARITIES 39231, PP_COND_MULT 195587, PPA_RARITIES 196738, the ppBuyVehicle/vmCancelListing/vmBuyListing/_ppaWin cap sites, the bridge's condMult lookup at 207933 — and the claims it makes about other files are true where I could test them: OPS_ECON.transport really does exist with exactly startup/ratePerWorkerHr/salaryPerWorkerHr/maxWorkers/yields/inputs and no rig fields, index.js:1239 really does pass condMult as a function (the recorded audit-blindness bug), _ppaWin:196915 really does assign `p.lot.length` while every sibling scans for the first free slot, and the mirrored PP_VEHICLE_NAMES list really is 20 names matching. Against the bar file it is denser in the dimension the repo values most: four recorded rejected designs (the PP_VEHICLE_NAMES merge, lotSlots enforcement, threading condMult as a parameter, summing garage tiers), a measured past bug with its reproduction, a drift alarm that reports itself unfed, and an explicit statement of what [] does not prove. One defect survives: the file's own GREP HYGIENE rule is asserted more broadly than it is kept.
biggest_gap: GREP HYGIENE rule 1 asserts that index.html's top-level consts 'appear in PROSE only, never in an expression and never inside a string this file can print', and the parenthetical generalises it to auditRigs()'s diagnostics — but four of the audit's problem strings print exactly such names: PP_VEHICLE_NAMES (L730), PP_CONDITIONS (L753), and PP_COND_MULT (L745, L765, L770). The file's own L328 calls PP_COND_MULT 'a top-level `const` in index.html — a global LEXICAL binding', so these are in scope by its own definition. Worse, the discipline is applied to exactly one of the four: L656 contorts around the rarity const into 'the top-level rarity const — anchor is in the comment on this rule', which is the least actionable message in the file and sits three rules above one that names PP_COND_MULT in backticks. Either extend the rule to those four strings (each has a usable description at hand) or narrow rule 1 in writing to the CLAUDE.md globals-trap names it is really about, and delete the L656 contortion so that message names its authority like its siblings do.

builder_response: The criterion is an unqualified grep and the file was failing it literally at two comment lines, so I fixed it the way the critic specified: both references now read 'the paid Garage effects table (index.html ~164432)' and no warning text was lost. I did not stop at the rename, because the critic's real charge was inconsistency with the file's own discipline rather than the two hits themselves. So I added a GREP HYGIENE block that makes the omission an argued rule instead of an unexplained absence (a boundary check that returns comment hits is a manual review, not a check), and that names the cost of dropping the identifier and the substitute anchor that covers it. Then I ran the globals rule's own grep and found the same class of gap the critic had caught: RARITIES sat inside a runtime diagnostic string in auditRigs(), which is a non-comment line and therefore a literal violation of 'zero non-comment hits'. Fixed the same way, by moving the anchor into the comment above the rule. Both greps now come back clean.
